posts.title: On making a place you can return to
posts.summary: The best personal systems feel less like rules and more like familiar rooms.
posts.imageAlt: Laptop, notebook, and coffee on a desk
posts.body:
A workbench teaches you what a homepage rarely can: every tool earns its place by being used. The surface gathers marks, the edges soften, and the small arrangement of things begins to hold a memory of the work.

I think a personal practice needs that same kind of room. Not a perfect system, but a place that makes it easier to begin again.

For me, that place is somewhere between the shop and the screen, between the grain of a board and the blank page. The work becomes more honest when both sides are allowed to inform each other.

posts.title: The creative value of going somewhere else
posts.summary: A walk, a long train ride, and the ideas that show up once you stop asking for them.
posts.imageAlt: Mountain landscape in soft evening light
posts.body:
Leaving a familiar room changes the scale of your attention. A road becomes a line, a field becomes a composition, and a small detail on the side of the path becomes enough to carry home.

That is useful for making. Distance interrupts the habits that tell us what a thing is supposed to be before we have really looked at it.

I come back with fewer answers, which is usually the better material for beginning something new.

posts.title: A better relationship with unfinished work
posts.summary: Some projects need a deadline. Others need a little more time in the dark.
